title: The Black Death (1347–1351)
hook: a third of Europe dies; Jews are scapegoated, and Pope Clement VI condemns the killings

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dante, from a dark wood to the last line of paradise. Your line was the love that moves the sun. Did you find a star? Today's story is darker. Day eight hundred twenty-one.

A rumor travels faster than the sickness. In town after town along the trade roads, people are dying in their houses, and nobody can say why. Then someone says the wells have been poisoned. Someone else says who did it: the Jews. In some towns, Jewish families who had lived beside their Christian neighbors are driven out, or burned. The sickness keeps coming anyway. Today we look at that terrible season honestly, and at one voice that refused the lie: the Black Death.
screen: `A RUMOR FASTER THAN THE SICKNESS.` → `THE WELLS, AND A LIE.` → `ONE VOICE REFUSES IT.`

segments.voice: First, the sickness. A plague swept across Europe. Households were lost, and some towns couldn't bury their dead fast enough. Nobody understood how it spread. Fear went looking for a cause it could see. Second, the blame. In towns along the Rhine and elsewhere, Jewish communities were accused of poisoning wells. Mobs, and sometimes town councils, killed many of them. This happened in Christian towns, at the hands of Christians. The Church remembers it, and does not excuse it. Third, the pope. Clement the Sixth, living in Avignon, issued decrees against the killings. His argument rested on plain evidence: Jews were dying of the plague like everyone else, and it was striking places where no Jews lived at all, so the accusation made no sense. He ordered the clergy to protect Jews, and threatened with excommunication anyone who harmed them. His words did not stop every mob. But they named the lie. Fourth, the Gospel's own refusal. In John's Gospel, the disciples see a man born blind and ask whose fault it is. In the Douay-Rheims: "who hath sinned, this man, or his parents, that he should be born blind?" And Jesus answers: "Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents." He refuses to turn suffering into blame, even with it right in front of him. In a liturgy of repentance in Lent, Pope John Paul the Second asked forgiveness for sins Christians had committed against the Jewish people. Remembering the plague years honestly is part of that.
screen: `FEAR LOOKS FOR A CAUSE.` · `A COMMUNITY BLAMED, AND KILLED.` · `THE PLAGUE KILLED JEWS TOO.` · `NEITHER HATH THIS MAN SINNED.` · then, large: `NO SCAPEGOATS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for those blamed in epidemics. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind people who have been blamed for a sickness, in history or in the news: a community, a nationality, a neighbor who got sick first. Hold them one at a time. Then notice, gently, whether any of that blame has ever lived in you. Don't argue with it. Just see it. If you pray, you can bring them to God in your own words, or hold Jesus' answer, neither hath this man sinned. If you don't, simply wish them safety. The bell holds the time.
The Black Death. The plague that swept medieval Europe, and the fear that turned on Jewish neighbors, which a pope condemned. Today's word.
Your line: no scapegoats. Today, when something goes wrong and the room starts looking for someone to blame, ask what actually happened before you ask who. Day eight hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: The Catholic Church remembers sins committed by Christians against the Jewish people in documents and acts of repentance, such as the Day of Pardon liturgy under Pope John Paul II, and Catholic teaching since the Second Vatican Council rejects blaming Jews collectively.

notes: Per the claims rule, the index hook's 'a third of Europe dies' is not stated in the voice; the scale is described only as chroniclers' reports of households lost and towns unable to bury their dead. Confirm acceptable.

Clement VI's decrees (July and September 1348) paraphrased: Jews dying of the plague too; plague striking places with no Jews; clergy ordered to protect; excommunication threatened. Confirm wording and citation.

Persecutions 'in towns along the Rhine and elsewhere', by mobs and sometimes town councils (e.g. Strasbourg). Confirm phrasing. The script names Christian responsibility plainly and avoids drama; please check tone.
Day of Pardon (Lent, 2000) referenced without date; confirm description.
